chapter: New Orleans, Havana and back to New York
title: The cooperative band's personnel and Romer as manager
summary: He names the trumpet section with Chris Griffin and Eddie Sauter and the rest of the cooperative band, and describes Romer's loose manager-booker role.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: We split. Incidentally, that band, the trumpet section's rather interesting. It was Chris Griffin, Eddie Sauter, and Tootie Camarata.
And the -- we just split. That was the end of the band.

Well, Root Bigadack was the piano player. Les Cooper was the saxophone, first saxophone. Frank Llewellyn was the trombone player. And Fred Follensby was the tenor man. And Jack Henderson was the other alto man. And -- I'll tell you who came around there, and wanted to sit in, was Johnny -- he was quite a popular singer a few years back and he disappeared -- Johnny -- he's a guitar player. Now his last name's gone. Anyway --

Oh, no, not Ray. I may think of it. Anyway, we had a guitar player by the name of Buford Turner, and it was a cooperative band, incidentally. So like I wasn't exactly responsible for what happened, you know. I was the guy up in front of it, but I mean we'd have our meetings, and when

they'd say don't play this and don't play that and the band would say no, we've got to play what we're going to play, and I'd say okay. You know. But that was the end of the big business cooperative band.
Well, Milton Romer booked your band, is that right? He was your manager or what?

He was the manager. In those days it was -- it wasn't much of a definition of who was a manager and who was a booker. The laws weren't too stringent about that. Like he did this directly. It wasn't done through any office. He still had Ozzie Nelson, who was very big at the time, you know. He had a commercial radio program and doing this thing.
